title: Before the fall no delight ruled the will; the first sin had no delight before it
source_text: LXVIII. Itaque totum istud tribuit imbecillitati cuidam voluntatis per peccatum contractae, & quae inter peccati poenas numeranda est. Nec enim ante peccatum, juxta illius hypotheses, delectatio ulla voluntati dominabatur, & in alterutram partem illam flectebat ac determinabat, efficaciter ejus consensum eliciendo. Nam priusquam homo per peccatum integritate sua primaeva cecidisset, nulla terrenarum rerum delectatio voluntatem ejus ad malum sollicitabat & illiciebat; idque quoniam omnis ejusmodi delectatio nascitur ex concupiscentia, quae peccati fructus est. Ac proinde primum peccatum primi hominis sine delectatione praecedente perpetratum est. Delectatio quippe prima secuta est perversam voluntatem, non voluntas delectationem. Siquidem omnis repugnantia bonae voluntatis supplicium est malae; quod Deus creaturae rationali non infligit immeritae.
pass_a_gloss: LXVIII. Therefore he attributes all that to a certain weakness of the will contracted through sin, and which is to be numbered among the penalties of sin. For before sin, according to his hypotheses, no delight ruled the will, and bent and determined it to either side, by efficaciously eliciting its consent. For before man through sin fell from his primeval integrity, no delight of earthly things solicited and enticed his will to evil; and that because every delight of this kind is born from concupiscence, which is the fruit of sin. And therefore the first sin of the first man was committed without preceding delight. For delight first followed the perverse will, not the will delight. Since every resistance of the good will is the punishment of the evil one; which God does not inflict on a rational creature undeserving.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXVIII. So he ascribes all this to a weakness of the will contracted through sin, which is to be counted among the punishments of sin. On his assumptions, before sin no delight ruled the will, bending and determining it to one side or the other by effectively drawing out its consent.

Before man fell from his original integrity through sin, no delight in earthly things urged and enticed his will toward evil, since every such delight is born of concupiscence, which is the fruit of sin. The first sin of the first man was therefore committed with no delight going before it: the first delight followed the perverse will, not the will the delight. For every resistance to a good will is the punishment of an evil will, and God does not inflict it on a rational creature that has not deserved it.
